flowers, and vanished predecessors, addresses the cupbearer and God, values wine above empire and future paradise, describes a hellish shape breaking a wine flask, and presents the heart at the banquet of the Divinity tasting the wine of annihilation.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker tells Khayyam to turn from mosque, prayer, and fasting toward the tavern, intoxication, and wine.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Human earth or dust is said to become cups, bowls, and pitchers, or to fall on the tavern sill saturated with wine.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Roses bloom through the zephyrs, gladden the nightingale, and then quickly depart from the earth.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A collective group speaks as lovers and drunkards, reunited in the tavern, freed from pain, and overcome by wine or the wine of love.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker questions the value of living one or two hundred years and says that the newborn soon disappears, while predecessors are dust or wind.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The cypress and lily are described as free because the cypress has tongues but remains mute and the lily has many hands but keeps them empty.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The cupbearer is asked to place delicious wine or crucible.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A filthy shape, neither man nor woman and clothed in a shirt made of the smoke of Hell, breaks a flask and spills ruby wine on the earth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The heart is admitted to the banquet of the idol identified as the Divinity after going out of itself and found Zoroaster's last followers in Persia and India and reported their existence, manners, and main beliefs to Europe.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Gabriel du Chinon saw the books of the Parsis and recognized that they were not all in the same language.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage states that the original holy writ was no longer understood except by means of translations and commentaries in another tongue.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Thomas Hyde made a systematic attempt to restore the history of the old Persian religion by combining Muslim writers' accounts with materials he treated as ancient Persian monuments.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The passage says Hyde's supposed ancient Persian monuments were actually recent compilations referring to the last stage of Parsiism.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hyde appealed to travelers to seek and procure the sacred books of the Parsis, and scholars afterward considered studying Parsiism in its own home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"George Boucher received a copy of the Vendidad Sadah from the Parsis in Surat, and Richard Cobbe brought it to England in 1723.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The manuscript was treated as unreadable, hung by an iron chain to the wall of the Bodleian XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X; lines 3781-3882","start":"3781","end":"3882","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage explains how animals, celestial bodies, and humans are classified under Ormazd/Ahura Mazda or Ahriman; describes storm-tale imagery in which gods and fiends take animal or object forms; treats killing Ahrimanian creatures as an attack on Ahriman; describes TLrtrya's forms and celestial allies; and states that the righteous man of Asha receives a heavenly place and participates in end-time resurrection and renewal.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that animals are said to belong to Ormazd or Ahriman according to usefulness or harmfulness to humans, but it explains their original assignment as arising from divine or fiendish incarnation in storm tales.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage says the fiend is described as a serpent because the storm fiend surrounds the goddess of light or the milch cows of the raining heavens with cloud coils like a snake's folds.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage states that gods and fiends could be compared with, and transformed into, objects suggested by storm noise, lightning, streaming water, or the color and shape of clouds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Killing the Ahrimanian creatures called Khrafstras is presented as killing Ahriman himself and as a possible atonement for sin; killing an Ormazdean animal is presented as an abomination.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage notes that birds of prey were assigned to Ormazd because lightning imagery described the god as moving on raven wings and with a hawk's flight, even though this classification could conflict with an expected usefulness principle.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"TLrtrya, conqueror of Apaosha, is described in mythic tales as a boar with golden horns, a horse with yellow ears, and a beautiful youth; because he was compared to a shining star, the stars stand with him on Ahura's side while the planets pass into Ahriman's army.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The passage states that humans belong to Ormazd or Ahriman according to deeds; a man of Asha helps Ormazd through sacrifice, good thoughts, words, and deeds, spreading life, and destroying Ahriman's creatures.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The man of Asha is exemplified by the Athravan priest, the Rathaejta warrior, and the Vastryo husbandman; contrary figures are named as Drva;//j, Anashavan, and Ashemaogha.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The man of Asha who has lived for Ahura Mazda is said to have a seat near him in heaven, and at the end of time the dead rise and live a new happy life on earth freed from evil and death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A footnote states that the Iranian worship of the Fravashis developed from the worship of the Pitrs and describes the Fravashi as an immortal part of the individual that existed before life and survived after death.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ormazd / Ahura Mazda / Ahura","description":"The beneficent divine side to whom Ormazdean animals heaven.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Ahriman","description":"The hostile divine or fiendish side; Khrafstras are his creatures, and as unclean through relationship with the deceased.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Angra Mainyu is addressed as mischievous and away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Airyama-ishyo is to be chanted four times, with an invocation for beloved Airyaman to come A quotation from Elizabeth Cookson presents customs, creeds, tales, songs, and superstitions as evidence for past mental life. The author then applies this framework to Zulu tales, claiming they show traces of a higher past, evidence of intellectual and tender feeling, and practical value for learning language, traditional lore, and missionary translation work.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that children's tales are not simply inventions of a child's intellect or made only to please a child's fancy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage says that careful comparison of these tales with corresponding legends among other peoples may reveal unexpected relationships and a unity of human mental qualities.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A footnote says that a method like Rev. G. W. Cox's treatment of ancient Greek literature could turn many of these tales into Solar Myths and connect Greek and Zulu materials, or both with an earlier period.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Elizabeth Cookson is quoted as comparing customs and creeds to fossil remains for the historian.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Elizabeth Cookson is quoted as saying popular tales, songs, and superstitions preserve and reflect turns and modes of the river opens or divides, and he crosses.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After the tenth river has been crossed, all ten oxen have been disposed of, and Ulangalasenzantsi travels alone.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"An editorial note states that the names of the two kings reflect an eastern-shore geography in which the sea is below and the mountains are above, making the eastern rising sun the lower sun and the western setting sun the upper sun.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"An editorial note describes South African customs of respecting or sacrificing to rivers and concludes that Ulangalasenzantsi likely threw the oxen into the rivers as sacrifices to amatongo or river-gods.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ulangalasenzantsi","description":"A figure who says he will fetch his children, gathers ten oxen, travels toward Ulangalasenthla, and crosses ten rivers by casting oxen into them.","role_refs":["role:1","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Ulangalasenthla","description":"The figure with whom Ulangalasenzantsi's children are located; When the boy hears the pursuers near, he addresses Ubongopa-kamagadhlela and calls for standing still because enemies are killing them. The cattle stand still. The pursuers accuse the boy of magic, tell him to come down and stand away from the cattle, and repeatedly throw assagais at him; the assagais strike the ground instead of hitting him. The boy jeers at them and asks for an assagai to stab at them. After further failed throws, the pursuers say they are worsted and invite him to try. A footnote compares the failed missiles with a scene in the Odyssey where Minerva turns aside weapons hurled at Ulysses.","language":"Zulu with English translation","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A ruler summons the whole tribe and orders them to follow the boy so that he may be Ubongopa-kamagadhlela.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the boy's speech, he calls for standing still and says they are being killed by thieves of another tribe.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The cattle stand still after the boy speaks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The pursuers tell the boy to stand still so they may kill him and accuse him of having practised magic for a long time.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The boy comes content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l33902-l34009","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"I ZING  AX  EK  W AN  E . / UMAMBA. / IZINGA  NEK  WANE. / UMAMBA.; lines 33902-34009","start":"33902","end":"34009","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Umamba asks his father for cattle so he can go to a damsel’s father for marriage arrangements. He travels with cattle and young men.
